title: ‘Structural divergence’ in China’s economy exposes a growing problem
gist: The PBoC's new term 'jiegou fenhua' (structural divergence) describes China's two-speed economy: record exports and manufacturing dominance alongside deep household retrenchment, both rooted in Beijing's 2020 pivot of capital away from real estate. The article weighs whether this pivot was innocent rebalancing or a deliberate strategy to build geopolitical leverage via manufacturing and export controls.

insights.claim: The People's Bank of China used the term 'jiegou fenhua' (structural divergence) in its July 2026 statement to describe an economy running at two different speeds: booming manufacturing and exports versus depressed household spending and sentiment.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Official acknowledgment of a bifurcated economy signals Beijing may be preparing new targeted stimulus for households rather than broad-based easing; watch PBoC statements for policy follow-through.
insights.quote: What it means is that the economy is running at two different speeds.
insights.locator: China’s policymakers can compete with the best when it comes to euphemism

insights.claim: This divergence is not new: Chinese household gloom has deepened continuously since the pandemic ended, over almost the exact same period that Chinese manufacturers have been accelerating their capture of global export market share.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: A multi-year, not cyclical, divergence implies the household weakness is structural and unlikely to self-correct without a policy shift on property or domestic demand.
insights.locator: This is by no means a new phenomenon

insights.claim: China posted a $125 billion trade surplus in June 2026, its largest monthly trade surplus ever recorded.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: A record surplus of this size raises the odds of renewed trade friction with major partners, particularly the US and EU, as global rebalancing pressure builds.
insights.quote: China’s $125 billion trade surplus for the month of June, for example, was its largest ever.
insights.locator: China’s $125 billion trade surplus for the month of June

insights.claim: Chinese export volumes have been growing at close to 15% year-on-year, partly boosted by rising AI investment, while global import volumes are growing at less than 5%; because export growth has outpaced global import growth without interruption since early 2023, China's global export market share has been rising continuously over that period.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: A persistent, multi-year gain in Chinese export share signals AI-driven manufacturing capacity is a durable competitive edge, not a one-off cyclical bump, and a source of ongoing friction with import-competing economies.
insights.locator: Consider this: in recent months, the year-on-year growth rate

insights.claim: Chinese retail sales growth was just 0.7% over the first six months of 2026, compared with over 4% in the United States over the same period.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Near-stagnant retail sales growth despite a booming export sector confirms domestic consumption is not a near-term growth lever for China-exposed consumer plays.
insights.locator: The flipside of this is very weak retail sales growth

insights.claim: The urban household savings rate in China is now running close to 40%, up from roughly 33% before the pandemic, a level the article calls already extraordinarily high pre-pandemic.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Elevated precautionary savings represent latent consumer purchasing power that could unlock significant demand if confidence is restored, but there is no current catalyst for that shift.
insights.locator: the data shows that the savings rate of urban households

insights.claim: Growth in China's total social financing, the country's broadest measure of credit to the economy, has set new all-time lows in each of the last three months, indicating households and businesses are reluctant to borrow.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Collapsing credit demand despite an export boom suggests monetary easing alone will struggle to revive domestic activity, since the constraint is confidence, not credit availability.
insights.locator: few want to borrow: the growth rate of total social financing

themes.theme: Property collapse as the structural root cause

insights.claim: In 2020, Chinese authorities made a deliberate decision to direct capital away from the property sector, on which the economy had relied heavily since the Global Financial Crisis, and towards manufacturing instead.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: This 2020 policy choice, not the pandemic itself, is identified as the root cause of today's divergence, meaning any reversal would require Beijing to actively re-open capital flows to property.
insights.locator: What connects them is the decision that the authorities took in 2020

insights.claim: The average of real estate prices across 70 Chinese cities, published monthly by the National Bureau of Statistics, fell again in June 2026 and is now more than 20% below its peak in the summer of 2021; the decline is still ongoing.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
entities: National Bureau of Statistics of China
insights.so_what: A still-unresolved, five-year property decline of over 20% implies the wealth-effect drag on Chinese consumption has further to run before stabilizing.
insights.locator: the average of real estate prices in 70 cities

insights.claim: Real estate investment had come to account for around a quarter of Chinese GDP before Beijing's 2020 rebalancing away from the sector.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: The scale of the prior property dependence (roughly 25% of GDP) explains why its unwinding has been severe enough to reshape the entire growth model rather than being a contained sectoral correction.
insights.locator: since real estate investment had come to account for around a quarter

insights.claim: The property price decline has produced a 'negative wealth effect' in which falling real estate values, given that housing is Chinese households' main asset, erode financial confidence and make households more reluctant to spend.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Because the wealth effect operates through the asset households hold most, any recovery in consumer spending is likely to require a bottom in property prices first, not just income support.
insights.quote: This has led to a ‘negative wealth effect’: falling real estate prices cause households to lose confidence and make them more nervous about spending.
insights.locator: Chinese households have taken a huge knock to their financial confidence

themes.theme: Transmission mechanisms linking property collapse to export strength

insights.claim: Weak domestic spending mechanically boosts China's exports because Chinese firms turn to foreign markets when domestic consumers are unwilling to spend, and this dynamic has persisted continuously since real estate prices began falling.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: This mechanism implies Chinese export strength and weak domestic demand are two sides of the same coin, so trade partners should not expect export intensity to ease until domestic consumption revives.
insights.locator: Chinese firms look for markets abroad when domestic consumers are unwilling to spend

insights.claim: Weak domestic demand has kept Chinese inflation very low relative to trading partners, and this inflation differential has driven a roughly 15% depreciation in China's trade-weighted, inflation-adjusted (real) exchange rate since early 2022, reinforcing export competitiveness.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: A real effective depreciation driven by low inflation rather than currency intervention is a durable competitiveness edge that is harder for trade partners to counter via tariffs on currency manipulation grounds.
insights.locator: China’s trade-weighted, inflation-adjusted exchange rate has depreciated

themes.theme: Deliberate strategy or accident: geopolitical leverage

insights.claim: There are two competing explanations for why Beijing induced the property collapse: a geopolitically innocent one (necessary rebalancing away from an oversized real estate sector) versus one centered on geopolitics (deliberately building manufacturing dominance as leverage).
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Which explanation is correct determines whether China's export dominance is a side effect that could be moderated by future stimulus, or a persistent strategic choice investors should price in as structural.
insights.locator: one has to wonder why that collapse was induced by policymakers

insights.claim: The strong US economic recovery after the 2008 crisis ('US exceptionalism'), driven partly by budget deficits and technology investment, may have convinced Chinese policymakers during the 2010s to reinforce their commitment to establishing China as a manufacturing powerhouse in response.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: If correct, this reframes China's manufacturing buildout as a response to a specific historical rivalry with the US, suggesting the strategy is unlikely to be abandoned while US-China competition continues.
insights.quote: It is worth suggesting, at least, that this episode of US exceptionalism might have convinced Chinese policymakers to reinforce their commitment to establishing China as a ‘manufacturing powerhouse’
insights.locator: One trend that Beijing won’t have failed to notice

insights.claim: China's manufacturing dominance has translated into geopolitical leverage through export controls; the clearest example is the rare earth export licensing regime Beijing announced in April 2025, which pushed the Trump administration to back down from its threatened 145% tariff on Chinese goods.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Rare earths have been proven as an effective bargaining chip against US tariff threats; investors should watch for further use of export licensing as a negotiating tool in future US-China trade disputes.
insights.quote: the rare earth export licensing regime Beijing announced in April last year, which pushed the Trump administration to climb down from its threat of a 145 per cent tariff on Chinese goods
insights.locator: the rare earth export licensing regime Beijing announced in April last year

insights.claim: In March 2026 the Chinese Academy of Sciences identified 63 strategically sensitive technologies that could become eligible for future export restrictions, including quantum devices, aerospace engineering components, biotechnology and electromagnetic catapult systems.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: This list is a roadmap for where Beijing could next escalate export controls beyond rare earths; investors in quantum, aerospace, and biotech supply chains with China exposure should monitor for new restriction announcements.
insights.quote: identified 63 strategically sensitive technologies that might be eligible for effective export restrictions, including quantum devices, aerospace engineering components, biotechnology and electromagnetic catapult systems
insights.locator: In March this year the Chinese Academy of Sciences
